title: Versatile Verb
bodyHtml:
In the left column below appear sentences in Waama, or Yoabu, a Gur language of Benin spoken by roughly 50,000 people. These sentences appear in the writing system of the language. You do not need to know how the writing system's letters are pronounced to solve this problem. In the right column below, the translations of these sentences in English appear in a scrambled order.

WaamaEnglish (scrambled)
1. Cando dɛbite kpi, o ǹ faa o suka.A. The tree fell in the forest.
2. Tando dori.B. A car passed by earlier.
3. N pe saaki ti yete.C. I went to my friend's house.
4. Bika kɔɔsi kɔɔka.D. The child fell.
5. Soosada kaate.E. Marie lost the money, but she found it.
6. Suka kpi.F. It rained.
7. Ba kaate tiibu band.G. My hen went to Yooto's house.
8. N yeentire n daaso.H. My wife swept our house.
9. Bisu yɔkɔɔti.I. The children had fun.
10. Tiibu dori puŋa mii.J. Tchando's neighbor died, and he inherited his car.
11. N taka n daaso yete.K. They gathered under the tree.
12. Maari dikitifa pei, o ǹ fa piisi.L. I hurt my friend.
13. Suka miiki pɔmpɔmma.M. The soldiers assembled.
14. Bika dori.N. The car broke down.
15. N kɔɔka taka Yooto yete.O. The child sold the hen.

C2. One of the verbs you encountered in the sentences in the left column above would be used by speakers of this language in all 4 sentences below, each of which is translated into English. Which of the verbs you encountered above is that verb?

N tokore verb'My shirt is torn.'
Yaama verb'The matter is settled.'
O beere verb'He lost his fame.'
Yima verb'The water is frozen.'

questions.partPrompt: Translate the following Waama sentences into English.

acceptedVariants: The friend of Marie inherited it.

hints.text: Start with the shortest Waama sentences and the shortest English translations. A two-word Waama sentence can only match a very short English sentence, and once you have pinned a word down you can carry it into the longer sentences that reuse it.

Waama is subject-verb-object, but words that English puts before a noun come after it here: location words work like 'tree under' rather than 'under the tree', and possession is shown just by putting the owner in front of the thing owned, with no extra marker at all. There are also no words for 'a' or 'the'. Keep in mind that one verb can cover a whole family of English meanings.

Look at the two noun shapes kɔɔka and kɔɔsu. They differ only in their ending, and that -a versus -u swap is the difference between one and more than one. Spotting that pattern lets you tell singulars from plurals in words you have never seen written out in both forms.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: use the short sentences as a foothold

Several Waama sentences are only two words long: Tando dori., Suka kpi., Soosada kaate., Bisu yɔkɔɔti., Bika dori.. On the English side, the short sentences are 'It rained.', 'The car broke down.', 'The soldiers assembled.', 'The children had fun.', 'The child fell.'

Notice that dori shows up in two of the short sentences and also in the longer Tiibu dori puŋa mii. The English sentence 'The tree fell in the forest.' is the only long sentence built on 'fell', so dori must mean 'fell' and tiibu must be 'tree'. That immediately splits the two dori sentences: one has Tando as subject and one has Bika. English gives us 'The child fell.' and 'It rained.' — and in Waama 'it rained' is literally 'rain fell', so tando is 'rain' and bika is 'child'.

Step 2: chain the vocabulary through the longer sentences

Once bika is 'child', the sentence Bika kɔɔsi kɔɔka. can only be about a child doing something to something, and 'The child sold the hen.' fits. So kɔɔsi is 'sold' and kɔɔka is 'hen'. That in turn helps with N kɔɔka taka Yooto yete., which contains 'hen' plus a name, matching the English sentence about a hen going to Yooto's house. Two useful facts fall out: n means 'my', and yete means 'house'.

The word yete then appears again in N pe saaki ti yete. and N taka n daaso yete., which line up with the two remaining house sentences ('My wife swept our house.' and 'I went to my friend's house.'). Compare the two: both start with N, but in one it is 'my' modifying pe 'wife' and in the other it is the subject 'I'. The verb taka means 'went to' — it swallows the English preposition 'to' all by itself.

Step 3: postpositions

A postposition is a little word that does the job of an English preposition but sits after the noun. In Tiibu dori puŋa mii. the literal order is 'tree fell forest in', so mii is 'in'. In Ba kaate tiibu band. the order is 'they gathered tree under', so band is 'under' and ba is 'they'. The same verb kaate covers both 'gathered' and 'assembled'.

Step 4: possession and the conjunction

There is no possessive marker in Waama at all. 'Marie's friend' is simply Maari daaso, and 'Yooto's house' is Yooto yete, exactly the way English says 'garage door' without adding anything. Also, in the two-clause sentences the joining word ǹ comes after the subject of the second clause, not at the front of it, and it can mean either 'and' or 'but' depending on context. And when the object is a pronoun, it comes before the verb: o ǹ fa piisi is literally 'she but it found'.

Step 5: the versatile verb (C2)

The four C2 sentences are about a shirt tearing, a matter being settled, fame being lost, and water freezing. What do those have in common? Each describes something coming to an end. In the main data one verb already covers both a person dying (in the Tchando sentence) and a car breaking down (Suka kpi.) — that verb's real meaning is 'come to an end', which is exactly the thread running through all four C2 sentences.

Step 6: plurals (C4)

The list gives 'child' and 'children' as bika and bisu: the singular ends in -a, the plural in -u, and the consonant before it shifts from k to s. Applying the same pattern, 'hen' kɔɔka becomes 'hens' kɔɔsu, and 'car' suka becomes 'cars' susu. That is how you read the plural task sentences, whose nouns look unfamiliar at first glance.

Step 7: building your own sentences (C3)

To translate into Waama, take the English sentence apart and reassemble it Waama-style: subject first, then verb, then object, with any preposition moved behind its noun and no articles anywhere. 'played in the rain' becomes 'played rain in', using the verb that the data glosses as 'had fun' — the same verb covers 'play'. And 'her' is just the pronoun o, which is not marked for gender, so it serves for 'his' and 'her' alike.
_reviewNotes: Keys taken from the official solution pages. Note a discrepancy in the source booklet: sentence 12 is printed on the problem page as 'Maari dikitifa pei, o ǹ fa piisi.' but appears in the solution table as 'Maari pei dikitifa, o ǹ fa piisi.' I transcribed the problem page as printed; the matching answer (E) is unaffected. The solution's letter list leaves item 15 blank, but the solution table shows 15 = G, which is what I used. Special characters to verify: ɛ (Cando dɛbite), ɔ (kɔɔsi, kɔɔka, yɔkɔɔti, pɔmpɔmma, kɔɔsu), ŋ (puŋa), ǹ (o ǹ). Point distribution is my own even split within parts (C1 0.2 x 15, C2 1, C3 1 x 3, C4 1 x 3 = 10); the booklet shows no per-part breakdown.
